title: My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell
gist: A WIRED reporter traced 1,735 Democratic fundraising texts since March 2022 (725 this year) meant for a relative who has given about $1,700 total, finding nearly half of this year's carried tracking codes pointing to Sterling Data Company, an AI-driven donor-data broker that rents records to multiple campaigns. Sterling's CEO calls high-frequency texting a 'necessary evil' and admits no contact database is perfect.

insights.claim: The reporter received 725 political fundraising texts this year, more than 190 in the first 20 days of October, and 21 on October 14 alone.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Election-season SMS volume is extreme and rising into elections.

insights.claim: Since March 2022 the reporter's phone received 1,735 political texts from 812 different phone numbers, nearly none meant for him.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Number rotation helps campaigns evade opt-outs and spam filtering.
insights.locator: For starters, I downloaded my Messages

insights.claim: Replying STOP 49 times since 2021 did not end the texts; after he opted out of Jon Ossoff's campaign in November 2025, 13 more Ossoff texts arrived from nine different numbers.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Opt-out mechanisms are ineffective across fragmented sender ecosystems, a TCPA litigation exposure.
insights.locator: For years, I diligently opted out.

insights.claim: The DSCC sent 60 texts this year (22 in the first 20 days of October) from 28 numbers to a recipient whose intended target had given it $5 once in 2020; the DCCC sent 41 for $8 received.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Solicitation intensity is decoupled from donor value.
insights.locator: The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone

insights.claim: The intended donor made roughly 160 contributions since 2017 totaling about $1,700, with a median gift of $6, and gave $51 this year while the reporter's phone got 725 texts asking for his money.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Small-dollar donors are hammered disproportionately to their giving.

insights.claim: The same first-person 'Cory' appeal arrived three times in under two hours from three different fundraising operations the day after Cory Booker's 25-hour Senate speech.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Shared lists mean duplicative, uncoordinated outreach.

insights.claim: Tracking codes in ActBlue-bound links revealed acquisition, peer-to-peer fundraising and rented-list tags, and the name 'Sterling' recurred across unrelated campaigns.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Link-level tracking metadata exposes the data supply chain of political fundraising.
insights.locator: Almost every text contained a link

insights.claim: Sterling Data Company uses AI to find likely Democratic donors and, per a 2022 Forbes report, built a database of about 30 million political donors with hundreds of details on some, including cars driven and Netflix viewing.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: AI-powered donor profiling relies on consumer data aggregated from brokers.
insights.locator: Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm

insights.claim: Nearly half of the 725 texts this year contained tracking codes appearing to reference Sterling, from dozens of PACs and campaigns including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico and Mark Kelly.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A single data vendor can propagate one bad record across the whole party ecosystem.
insights.locator: Of the 725 texts I’d received this year

insights.claim: FEC records show a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months from November 2023, and the DSCC paid Sterling roughly $250,000 this summer before another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Donor-list rentals are a material, recurring campaign spend.
insights.locator: FEC records show that a Biden

insights.claim: Sterling's CEO Martin Kurucz says high-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil because few people give, every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Economics of SMS fundraising ensure the spam volume persists.
insights.quote: High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,

insights.claim: Kurucz confirmed Sterling handles texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns, and says moderate-confidence matches are accurate enough to use because wrong numbers drop out when recipients do not engage.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Vendors tolerate mismatches as an acceptable cost, shifting burden to wrong-number recipients.

insights.claim: At least two people have won settlements from Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Misdirected political texting carries legal liability.
insights.locator: I found that there’s another way out
